newsitem.title: USA: Robinson memorabilia should get boost from anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Robinson memorabilia should get boost from anniversary.

text.p: Next month it will be 50 years since Jackie Robinson broke baseball's colour barrier, an event that changed sports as well as the nation, and the American merchandising machine is cranking into gear.

Uniforms, autographs, baseball cards and other items from Robinson's playing days have already risen in value, but will get a further boost from the anniversary and surrounding publicity, collectors and baseball historians said.

"He is undoubtedly one of the magic names in baseball," said Robert Lifson of Robert Edward Auctions, an auction house that specialises in baseball. "People appreciate his historical significance and that's why material related to him is so widely collected."
Robinson memorabilia can command eye-popping prices. His uniforms are worth $50,000 to $75,000, values reserved for a handful of players such as Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Ty Cobb.
"Based on the 50th anniversary, I'm sure the asking price for his uniforms will be going up," said Dick Dobbins, a baseball historian from northern California.
A Robinson-autographed ball can bring $1,000 to $2,500, depending on condition, well above prices for most players' from his era.
"For a Hall of Fame player who died in the 1970s, an autographed ball is normally $300 to $400," said Ken Felden, who's been collecting baseball items for 20 years.

Robinson, who played his first game with the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947, retired after the 1956 season. He was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1962 and died 10 years later of a heart attack at 53.

Major League Baseball is dedicating this season in honour of the 50th anniversary and President Clinton plans to join the celebration during an April 15 game between the New York Mets and the visiting Los Angeles Dodgers.
Being the first black in Major League Baseball has undoubtedly made his mementoes more valuable. But other factors have contributed.

He played for the Dodgers, whose move to Los Angeles after the 1957 season not only broke millions of hearts but created a cult of would-be collectors. And by all accounts he was a gentlemen, which has enhanced his standing with the public and has boosted the value of his memorabilia, experts said.
"I had the fortune of meeting him. He was pleasant, highly articulate, very bright. And that makes a difference to some people," Dobbins said.
In addition, many items from Robinson's playing days are simply rare. Due to paper-saving during the war, there were no baseball cards in 1947, his rookie year.
His most valuable card, a 1952 Topps, was not widely produced and has sold for about $8,000 in mint condition, experts said. In lesser condition, it fetches $2,000-$3,000.
The scarcity of cards and other old items will not stop millions of people from owning a piece of Robinson.

The items being made for the anniversary will include everything from two types of commemorative cards to $7 baseballs to $300 jerseys, according to Darci Ross, president of CMG Worldwide, the marketing and licensing company that has represented Robinson's family for about a year. It also handles Ruth, Gehrig, Billie Holiday and James Dean.

Ross said each licensee is carefully screened for quality and submitted for approval by Rachel, Jackie's widow. In addition, some sales will generate proceeds for the Jackie Robinson Foundation, established in 1973 to help needy black students gain college scholarships.
Still, the new items, while sure to be snatched up and loved by millions of people, are unlikely to appreciate over the years, the experts said.
"This new stuff is poison as far as investment potential," said Lifson at Robert Edward Auctions. "If you want to buy it, that's great, but don't kid yourself about reselling it."
Other valuable Robinson collectibles include autographs, such as those on personal checks, documents related to his career and other items released by the family over the years.
His Most Valuable Player award sold for $25,000 a few years ago in a private sale, according to Felden, the New Jersey-based collector.
Then there's the 13-card set issued by Bond Bread company in 1947, all of Robinson. Single cards fetch $500 or more; the whole set brought $13,000 at auction in 1991.
Felden said that aside from Ruth, Robinson was the most important figure in baseball.
"And some people would make a case for him being the most important athlete in any sport," he said. "He's an icon, and icons command money in the collectible market."
